title: What is accounts payable?
subtitle: Supplier debt - a burden, or a negotiating edge?
openingQuestion: Walmart is famous for paying suppliers late, 60-90 days. Is this good or bad for Walmart?
openingOptions: Bad, because it damages its reputation
Bad - Walmart is short of cash
Good - Walmart uses supplier money for free, improving FCF
explanation: Accounts payable is the amount a business still owes its suppliers, and it is an interest-free source of capital. A business with strong negotiating leverage can stretch out its payment days, using its supply chain's capital to fund its own operations - Walmart and Amazon are classic examples. But the same rising number can also mean the business is short of cash and paying late against its will, so it must be read alongside cash balances.

diagram.label: Paying late = using supplier capital for free

realWorldExample.description: Walmart is famous for negotiating 60-90 day payment terms with most suppliers while collecting cash from customers instantly - using supplier capital to fund its operations without any interest cost.

quiz.question: Accounts payable to suppliers is:
options: Money the company has prepaid to a supplier
Money the company owes a supplier
Salaries the company owes its employees
Money customers still owe the company, unpaid
quiz.explanation: Accounts Payable = a current liability, to be settled within 30-90 days.

quiz.question: A company buys 1 billion of goods from a supplier, unpaid. Effect:
options: Assets rise 1 billion, assets fall 1 billion
Assets rise 1 billion, liabilities rise 1 billion
Liabilities rise 1 billion, equity rises 1 billion
No effect on the balance sheet, since no cash has changed hands yet

quiz.question: AP is classified under:
options: Current assets
Equity
Long-term liabilities
Current liabilities
quiz.explanation: AP = payment due <12 months = a current liability.

quiz.question: Why does a company want to stretch out AP?
options: To hold onto cash longer, improving cash flow
To raise the company's Current Ratio
To get a discount on the goods purchased
To reduce the tax owed for that period
quiz.explanation: AP is free credit: receiving goods without yet paying for them = optimising cash flow.

quiz.question: How does rising AP affect the Current Ratio?
options: Raises the Current Ratio
Lowers the Current Ratio
Raises the Current Ratio because AP is an asset
Raises the Quick Ratio
quiz.explanation: CR = CA/CL. Rising AP → rising CL → falling CR.

quiz.question: Maximising AP to improve cash flow:
options: Correct, the longer it can be stretched the better
Wrong, because AP raises bank interest expense
Wrong, AP that's too high damages supplier relationships
Correct, because AP incurs no interest cost
quiz.explanation: A balance is needed: optimise cash but don't damage the supplier relationship.

quiz.question: Unpaid salaries are recorded as:
options: Current assets
Equity
Long-term liabilities
Current liabilities
quiz.explanation: Unpaid salaries = an obligation due soon = a current liability.

keyTakeaways: High AP = a strong business using supplier cash interest-free
DPO = AP / (COGS/365) - measures AP management efficiency
Balance: paying late is good, but not at the cost of the supplier relationship

practicePrompt.question: Walmart is famous for paying its suppliers 45-60 days late while collecting from customers almost instantly (direct retail sales). What advantage does this create for Walmart?
options: Walmart uses supplier money (high AP) as a form of interest-free credit to fund its operations, meaningfully improving free cash flow
This is a sign Walmart is in financial trouble and cannot afford to pay suppliers on time
This creates no financial benefit whatsoever, it's simply a management habit of the company
This is a breach of contract with suppliers and will cause lasting damage to the business relationship
practicePrompt.explanation: High AP at a strong business like Walmart means it's using supplier money as interest-free credit (receive goods, sell them and collect cash, then pay the supplier later) - a very effective way of optimising free cash flow (FCF), not a sign of weakness.

summary.keyIdea: High AP = a strong business using supplier cash interest-free
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: DPO = AP / (COGS/365) - measures AP management efficiency

application.title: Check the payment terms you're currently given
application.message: Check your most recent credit card or buy-now-pay-later bill: how many days of credit are you given before you have to pay? That's your own personal DPO, used interest-free.
application.secondary: Using this window correctly is an advantage, but paying late costs you the advantage and adds a penalty fee.

sections.text: Accounts Payable (AP) is the amount a business owes suppliers because it has purchased goods/services but not yet paid for them. It sounds like 'bad debt', but for a strong business, high AP is actually a subtle financial advantage.
Why paying suppliers late can be an advantage

When a business is large and reputable enough, it has the negotiating power to demand longer payment terms - 30, 60, even 90 days. During that time, the business keeps cash in hand to invest, cycle capital, or simply earn deposit interest, while still using the goods/services already received. This is essentially an 'interest-free loan' from the supplier.
DPO and the limits of the pay-late strategy

Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) = AP / (COGS / 365) - the average number of days a business takes to pay its suppliers. A high DPO is good for the buyer's cash flow, but if stretched beyond what's reasonable for the industry, suppliers may stop extending credit, deprioritise delivery, or raise prices to offset the risk - damaging the long-term partnership.

items: High DPO + good inventory turnover: a sign of strong negotiating power and skilled working-capital management
DPO rising suddenly along with other signs of trouble: the company may be short of cash, forced to delay payments
Compare DPO against DSO and DIO for a full picture of the cash cycle

sections.label: Telling the two scenarios apart
sections.text: Rising AP isn't automatically good or bad. You also need to check: is operating cash flow positive, is the company paying its loans on schedule, and how long has this trend lasted - to distinguish 'skilled negotiator' from 'running out of cash'.

left.label: High AP from strength
left.text: Walmart, Amazon: market power lets them negotiate slow payment without hurting the supplier relationship

right.label: High AP from weakness
right.text: A small business in liquidity trouble is forced to delay payment, which can risk losing suppliers

lines: AP is a double-edged sword - good when it's strategy, bad when it's forced.
DPO needs to be read alongside DSO and DIO to understand the full capital cycle.
Skilled businesses optimise all three indicators at once to reduce their working-capital needs.
